<ConflictType> — Evidence shows both positive localized effects and null/negative overall effects, indicating genuine disagreement

The retrieved evidence clusters into two incompatible camps: several sources report statistically significant crime reductions in specific contexts (e.g., parking lots, residential car parks, and targeted neighborhood programs), while others find no statistically significant effect overall and even increases in some places. High-credibility reviews (d2, d5) conclude that CCTV alone often fails to reduce crime, contradicting localized success stories (d3, d4) and context-dependent claims (d1). This mutual exclusivity within the same scope and time window matches the “Conflicting opinions and research outcomes” label.

Cameras can reduce crime in specific contexts such as parking lots and residential car parks, with reported reductions around 37% in car parks and 12% in residential areas [d1,d3]. A neighborhood program using cameras reported even larger drops (robbery −45%, burglary −45%, theft from autos −62%, total −35%) [d4]. However, broader reviews find that CCTV implemented alone or with one other intervention does not produce a statistically significant overall reduction in crime [d2,d5]. Some studies even report no effect or slight increases in certain cities [d5]. Effectiveness appears to depend heavily on coverage, placement, maintenance, and publicization [d2,d6].
